feedback: If 403,072 is read as 'forty-three thousand...', the ten-thousands column was skipped: point to that empty column and say its 0 holds the place so the number is four hundred AND three thousand.
If 'four hundred thousand and seven' is written 400,700 or 4,000,007, rebuild it period by period (400 | 007) and count that each period has exactly three digits.
Dictating zero-heavy numbers and asking the learner to place the placeholder 0 themselves surfaces the empty-column error directly.
When forms are linked, changing the numeral should make the words and expanded form update; a mismatch shows a group or zero was read wrongly.
activities.intendedInsight: A six-digit number is read and built as two three-digit groups; internal zeros are placeholders that hold a column empty, and that empty column still needs its 0 so the magnitude stays correct.
learnerActions: Build a six-column place-value chart split by a comma into a thousands period and a ones period (e.g. 403 | 072), and add a millions column when showing 1,000,000, which needs seven digits.

Enter or read a number and keep three linked forms in sync: the grouped numeral (403,072), the number name ('four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two') and expanded form (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2).
Read the number by chunks, one period at a time, rather than reciting single digits.
Work deliberately on zero-heavy numbers: write 500,006; write 'four hundred thousand and seven' as a numeral (400,007); read 403,072 aloud.
Place each number on a 0-1,000,000 number line and tie it to a real quantity such as a city's population.
activities.title: Periods-based number translator to a million

feedback: If 543,801 is called larger because 801 > 301, redirect to the first place that differs when scanning from the left: the thousands place decides it (8 > 3).

If ordering is done by the first digit alone, or numbers with different digit counts are compared by lining up their left ends, align the numbers by place value (right-aligned) and compare column by column from the highest place until a difference appears. Comparing digit counts first is valid for whole numbers: more digits means larger.
Reading each number aloud by periods first helps confirm which place is which before comparing.
activities.intendedInsight: When numbers are aligned by place value (right-aligned), magnitude is decided by the highest place at which two numbers differ, not by left-alignment, the first digit alone, or the final digits. For whole numbers written without leading zeros, a number with more digits is always larger (100,000 > 99,999), and this is the same rule applied to an extra highest place.
learnerActions: Compare pairs such as 548,301 and 543,801, aligning them by place and scanning from the highest place first.
State which single place decides the comparison and stop there (here the thousands digit: 8 > 3, so 548,301 > 543,801).
Order a set of four six-digit numbers from smallest to largest, justifying each step by place value.
Include pairs that differ only in a middle place so the deciding digit is not at either end.
activities.title: Compare and order six-digit numbers from the highest place

feedback: If a tens digit is expanded as 7 instead of 70, name its place aloud and add the parts: 400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2 rebuilds to 403,009, not 403,072.
Always sum the expanded parts to confirm they reconstruct the original numeral.
activities.intendedInsight: Each digit's contribution equals its face value times its place value; dropping the place multiplier changes the number.
learnerActions: Decompose a six-digit number into place-value parts, naming each digit with its place ('7 tens = 70', not '7').
Rebuild the number by adding the parts back and check it matches the original numeral.
Compare a correct expansion (400,000 + 3,000 + 70 + 2) with a face-value error (400,000 + 3,000 + 7 + 2) and explain which digit is wrong and why.
activities.title: Expanded form by place value, not face value

feedback: If the spoken reading is correct but the written numeral drops a zero, compare the two period-by-period to find the missing placeholder.

If your class's naming convention uses 'and' (as in 'four hundred and three thousand and seventy-two'), say it only within a period's value, not as a substitute for a missing group. Many US curricula leave 'and' out of whole-number names, so follow the convention your materials use.
activities.intendedInsight: Fluent oral reading by groups and accurate written capture of the same number reinforce each other, and real contexts make the magnitude meaningful.
learnerActions: Hear or read a real large quantity (a city's population, a distance) and read the numeral back aloud by periods.
Then write the numeral you heard, placing any internal zeros as placeholders.
Discuss what the number means at that magnitude using the number line.
activities.title: Read big numbers aloud in a real context
